title: Same Text After Backspaces
statement:
Two strings a and b record keystrokes typed into empty text boxes. Lowercase letters are typed as they are; the character # is a backspace that deletes the character just before the cursor. A backspace on an empty box does nothing.

Return true if both boxes end up showing the same text, and false otherwise.

examples.why: The b and the d are both erased, so both boxes show "ac".
The second backspace in a hits an empty box and does nothing. Both boxes show "y".
The boxes show "a" and "ca". Matching from the end, the a's agree, but b still has a c left over.

constraints: a and b contain only lowercase letters and '#'
hints: The simple way: replay each string into a stack of characters and compare the results. Can you avoid the extra memory?
Read from the end. A backspace affects only characters to its left, so walking right to left you always know how many upcoming characters to skip.
Use one pointer per string, each with a skip counter. Move each pointer to its next character that survives, compare the two, and repeat. Both must run out at the same time.

explain.intuition:
Replaying the keystrokes into a stack is direct: push letters, pop on #. That costs O(n) memory.

To use O(1) memory, read backwards. From the right, a # says "skip the next letter you meet", so you keep a counter of pending skips. With one pointer per string, find the next surviving character in each and compare. This is how an editor could compare two undo histories without rebuilding the documents.
steps: Set i and j to the last index of a and b.
Move i left to the next surviving character: on # add a skip, on a letter with skips pending use one up, otherwise stop. Do the same for j.
If both pointers ran off the start, return true. If only one did, or the characters differ, return false.
Otherwise step both pointers left once and repeat.
pitfalls: Letting a backspace on an empty box go negative and then eat a later letter.
Stopping when one string runs out and returning true. The other may still have surviving characters, like the c in the third example.
Building new strings with repeated slicing, which is O(n²).

solutions.title: Replay into a stack
solutions.idea: Push letters, pop on '#', then compare the two results.

solutions.title: Two pointers from the end
solutions.idea: Walk both strings right to left, skipping characters that a later backspace erases, and compare survivors one pair at a time.

followups: Add a second key that deletes the character after the cursor, with arrow keys to move it. Does reading from the end still work?
Compare many keystroke logs at once and group the ones that produce the same text.
